notes: \cpara{Quotes the opening exchange of the dialogue in ``Disputing Definitions.''}
\cpara{Recalls losing the feel for why anyone would argue like Albert and Barry, while writing their dialogue.}
\cpara{Gives the sentence that restored the feel: ``Either the falling tree makes a sound, or it does not!''}
\cpara{Shows that ``P or not-P'' can fail for English sentences, with two stock cases: the liar sentence, and a question that presupposes something false.}
\cpara{Grants that a classical logician can keep ``P or not-P'' as a theorem, for example by denying that the liar is a sentence.}
\cpara{Concludes that such rescues take subtlety, so ``Either it does or it doesn't!'' cannot be applied blindly.}
\cpara{Introduces the arithmetic analogy: ``2 + 2 = X'' is not simply true or false if X changes.}

\cpara{The thesis: ``P or not-P'' requires that P mean the same thing in both halves. The error described has an old name that the post does not use. The fallacy of equivocation is ``an argument which exploits the ambiguity of a term or phrase which has occurred at least twice in an argument, such that on the first occurrence it has one meaning and on the second another meaning'' (\textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}, ``Fallacies''). Aristotle listed it among the fallacies that depend on language. The post gives the error a new name and extends it to words, like ``left'' below, whose meaning is set by context.}
\cpara{Explains the notation: C++'s ``::'' names which package's Sound is meant.}
\cpara{Notes that two people may check that they mean the same event and forget to check that they mean the same concept.}
\cpara{The clearest case in the post: which side of the street is ``the left'' depends on the direction of travel, a variable no one states.}
\cpara{Says that such context-dependent words are hard to handle in programs that parse language.}

\cpara{The example shows a different ambiguity from the one it is given for. The question ``Bob's or Martin's?'' is the question of whom ``his'' refers to, and the sentence states that variable openly with ``his.'' The same question arises in ``Martin told Bob the building was near his house,'' where no word like ``left'' occurs. The grocery-store example above does show a hidden variable in ``left'' itself.}
\cpara{Warns that the hidden variables are rarely marked, as the Z in ``Z + 2 = 6'' is.}

\cpara{Collects three sources of a shifting question: two concepts under one name, two events in one mental file, one word read in different contexts. The claim that this makes reality feel changeable rests on the account in ``How An Algorithm Feels From Inside''; see the notes there on the evidence for it.}
\cpara{Restates the previous paragraph: a hidden variable makes reality feel unstable.}
\cpara{Attributes this confusion to ``undergraduates (and postmodernist professors)'' and names or quotes none of them.}

\cpara{The quoted speech is the author's own composition, and its analysis is ``left as an exercise to the reader.'' So the post does not show which hidden variable the example contains, or how naming it would settle the matter.}
\cpara{Corrects a sentence of the author's own draft, correctly: a formula with a free variable, like ``2 + 2 = X,'' has no truth value at all, not a variable one.}
\cpara{Ends by saying the error returns even for those who know better, because of how the algorithm feels from inside.}
